{{Short description|Dual to the Dirac spinor}}
In [[quantum field theory]], the '''Dirac adjoint''' defines the [[dual vector space|dual]] operation of a [[Dirac spinor]].  The Dirac adjoint is motivated by the need to form well-behaved, measurable quantities out of Dirac spinors, replacing the usual role of the [[Hermitian adjoint]].

Possibly to avoid confusion with the usual [[Hermitian adjoint]], some textbooks do not provide a name for the Dirac adjoint but simply call it "{{math|{{mvar|ψ}}}}-bar".

== Definition ==

Let <math>\psi</math> be a [[Dirac spinor]].  Then its Dirac adjoint is defined as

:<math>\bar\psi \equiv \psi^\dagger \gamma^0</math>

where <math>\psi^\dagger</math> denotes the [[Hermitian adjoint]] of the spinor <math>\psi</math>, and <math>\gamma^0</math> is the time-like [[gamma matrices|gamma matrix]].

== Spinors under Lorentz transformations ==

The [[Lorentz group]] of [[special relativity]] is not [[compact space|compact]], therefore [[Spin representation|spinor]] [[Representations of the Lorentz group|representation]]s of [[Lorentz transformation]]s are generally not [[unitary operator|unitary]].  That is, if <math>\lambda</math> is a [[projective representation]] of some Lorentz transformation,

:<math>\psi \mapsto \lambda \psi,</math>

then, in general,

:<math>\lambda^\dagger \ne \lambda^{-1}.</math>

The Hermitian adjoint of a spinor transforms according to

:<math>\psi^\dagger \mapsto \psi^\dagger \lambda^\dagger.</math>

Therefore, <math>\psi^\dagger\psi</math> is not a [[Lorentz scalar]] and <math>\psi^\dagger\gamma^\mu\psi</math> is not even [[self-adjoint operator|Hermitian]].

Dirac adjoints, in contrast, transform according to

:<math>\bar\psi \mapsto \left(\lambda \psi\right)^\dagger \gamma^0.</math>

Using the identity <math>\gamma^0 \lambda^\dagger \gamma^0 = \lambda^{-1}</math>, the transformation reduces to

:<math>\bar\psi \mapsto \bar\psi \lambda^{-1},</math>

Thus, <math>\bar\psi\psi</math> transforms as a Lorentz scalar and <math>\bar\psi\gamma^\mu\psi</math> as a [[four-vector]].

== Usage ==

Using the Dirac adjoint, the [[probability current|probability four-current]] '''{{math|{{mvar|J}}}}''' for a spin-1/2 particle field can be written as

:<math>J^\mu = c \bar\psi \gamma^\mu \psi</math>

where {{math|{{mvar|c}}}} is the speed of light and the components of '''{{math|{{mvar|J}}}}''' represent the probability density {{math|{{mvar|ρ}}}} and the probability 3-current '''{{math|{{mvar|j}}}}''':

:<math>\boldsymbol J = (c \rho, \boldsymbol j).</math>

Taking {{nowrap|{{math|{{mvar|μ}} {{=}} 0}}}} and using the relation for [[gamma matrices]]

:<math>\left(\gamma^0\right)^2 = I,</math>

the probability density becomes

:<math>\rho = \psi^\dagger \psi.</math>
